# ML Compilers, From Zero, by Sharp Terminal

> A free, open-source, self-paced course where you build a machine learning compiler from scratch, in Python or OCaml. It is inspired by the public syllabus of CMU 10-411, Compilers for Machine Learning, and is independent: not affiliated with CMU or George Hotz.

The compiler works on a small graph IR of UOps, written in a text format called .uir. Each week adds ops and a spec, and each week ends in a hands-on lab where a test suite grades your compiler against a reference implementation. It starts with two short steps (run a program, then write the interpreter that runs it) and goes through ten weeks: interpreting and simplifying, memory and rendering C, loops, tensors and shapes, autodiff and training on MNIST, fast CPU kernels, CUDA GPU kernels, tensor cores and flash attention, and running on several GPUs. Short primers on C, memory, tensors and matrix multiply appear just before the week that needs them, and complete beginners can learn Python or OCaml from scratch first. Every lesson asks you to guess before it explains, has quizzes with hints and answers, and has graded exercises that run in the browser editor. No GPU is needed: CUDA runs in an emulator.

Source code, tests and the reference compiler: https://github.com/wilsonmike/ml-compilers-course

## Start here

- [Build an ML compiler from scratch.](https://sharpterminal.com/site/): A free, self-paced course where you build a machine learning compiler in Python or OCaml. Start by interpreting add 2 3 and finish with CUDA kernels, tensor cores and training on several GPUs, with a...

## Start: run a program, then write the interpreter that runs it

- [Run your first program](https://sharpterminal.com/site/start/01-run-a-program): Before you build a compiler, meet the tiny language it will read. In this step you read a program, guess what it does, run it and change it. You don't need to know any programming yet.
- [Build the thing that runs it](https://sharpterminal.com/site/start/02-build-a-calculator): In step 1 the page ran your programs. Something had to read add 2 3 and come back with 5. That something is called an interpreter, and it is the first working piece of your compiler. You'll write a...

- [Your own types](https://sharpterminal.com/site/learn/ml-04-your-own-types): So far every value had a type OCaml gave you: int, string, a list. In this lesson you make your own types. Your compiler is built from two of them: a record that holds one step of a program, and a...

- [Decisions, loops and functions](https://sharpterminal.com/site/learn/py-02-decisions-loops): So far your programs run every line once, top to bottom. In P.1 you filled in functions that were already started. This lesson adds three things: functions you write from the first line, if, which...
- [Lists, dicts and sets](https://sharpterminal.com/site/learn/py-03-collections): So far each name has pointed at one value. Real programs keep many values together. Here you learn Python's collections: the list, the dict, the set and the tuple. Two of them are things your...

- [Pad, shrink, expand, stack](https://sharpterminal.com/site/week5/03-pad-shrink-expand): Four more ops that move numbers around without computing anything. You will grow a grid with a border of zeros, cut a piece out of it, repeat one row to fill a grid and join two rows into one grid...
- [Matmul and conv from movement](https://sharpterminal.com/site/week5/04-matmul-conv): By the end of this lesson you can write a matrix multiply and a convolution with no loops at all: a few shape moves, one mul and one reduce. These two operations do almost all the work in a neural...
- [Rangeify movement ops](https://sharpterminal.com/site/week5/05-rangeify-movement): A movement op computes nothing. In this lesson you teach rangeify what to do with one: change the index, then ask the source. Once it can, your compiler turns lesson 5.4's matmul into two plain...
- [Lab: movement ops](https://sharpterminal.com/site/week5/06-lab): In this lab your compiler learns grids. It takes values of any rank, runs reshape, permute, pad and shrink, and turns each of them into index arithmetic when it renders C. You build it in the order...

- [Automatic differentiation](https://sharpterminal.com/site/week6/03-autodiff): By the end of this lesson you can say how far a program's output moves when one input moves a little, and work that number out for every input in one pass. The number is called the gradient. Training...
- [Gradients through shapes](https://sharpterminal.com/site/week6/04-gradients-of-shapes): By the end of this lesson you can send a gradient backward through ops that change shape: sums, copies, pads, cuts and reorders. A model is mostly these ops, so the backward walk from lesson 6.3 has...
- [Reading data, and a program that learns digits](https://sharpterminal.com/site/week6/05-data-and-mnist): Until now, every number your programs used was typed into the program. In this lesson your compiler does something anyone would call machine learning: it trains a small model to read handwritten...
- [Lab: train MNIST](https://sharpterminal.com/site/week6/06-lab): In this lab your compiler learns enough to train a model. It gains the math ops, the sugar, gradient and buffers read from files. At the end, C that your compiler wrote reads handwritten digits it...

- [Threads: iterations at the same time](https://sharpterminal.com/site/week7/04-threads): Your machine has several processor cores, and so far your compiled code has used one of them. In this lesson a loop hands its iterations to all of them with axis=thread. You also learn the rule that...
- [Kernels and outlining: rendering a thread loop](https://sharpterminal.com/site/week7/05-kernels): Lesson 7.4 proved that a thread loop's iterations can run at the same time. C has no way to say that about a for loop. Here you turn the loop's body into a function that any core can call, and you...
- [Lab: fast kernels](https://sharpterminal.com/site/week7/06-lab): In this lab your compiler learns to obey a program's schedule. It unrolls upcast loops, checks that thread loops are safe, and moves each thread loop into its own function. At the end, the C it...

## Week 8: GPUs (blocks and threads, shared memory, rendering CUDA, getting a GPU)

- [How a GPU runs code](https://sharpterminal.com/site/week8/01-gpus): You'll be able to picture how a GPU runs a loop: as thousands of threads, grouped into blocks, with three kinds of memory. Your compiler needs this picture because this week it starts to write...
- [Global and local loops](https://sharpterminal.com/site/week8/02-global-and-local): On a GPU, thousands of threads run the same code at once, and each one must pick its own piece of the work. In this lesson you write that in .uir with two new kinds of loop: one for the blocks and...
- [Shared memory and barriers](https://sharpterminal.com/site/week8/03-shared-memory): So far every thread did its work alone. In this lesson the threads of one block work together: each puts a value in the block's shared memory, they all wait, and then each reads what the others put...
- [Rendering CUDA](https://sharpterminal.com/site/week8/04-rendering-cuda): Your compiler can check and run block and thread programs, and it can print C for a CPU. It has never printed code for a GPU. Here you learn the four small changes that turn the C you already print...
- [Getting a GPU, or not needing one](https://sharpterminal.com/site/week8/05-getting-a-gpu): You do not need a GPU to finish this course. Every correctness test in weeks 8 and 9 runs in an emulator on any computer. A real NVIDIA GPU adds one thing, the speed tests. This lesson helps you pick...
- [Lab: GPU kernels](https://sharpterminal.com/site/week8/06-lab): In this lab your compiler learns blocks and threads. It reads global and local loops, proves that no two threads write the same element, and prints CUDA with a new command, render-cuda. You need no...

- [Tensor cores](https://sharpterminal.com/site/week9/03-tensor-cores): A tensor core is a part of the GPU that multiplies two small 16×16 matrices in a single step. It was built because machine learning is mostly matrix multiply. By the end of this lesson you can write...

- [Flash attention](https://sharpterminal.com/site/week9/05-flash-attention): Attention is the step a language model spends most of its time in. Done the obvious way, it fills a table of scores far too big for a GPU's fast memory. You'll learn the one trick that lets a kernel...
- [Lab: fast GPU kernels](https://sharpterminal.com/site/week9/06-lab): In this lab your compiler learns to make GPU kernels fast. It keeps each thread's sums in registers, reads i8 memory and turns mma and warp loops into tensor-core CUDA. You need no GPU: the emulator...

- [Moving memory](https://sharpterminal.com/site/week10/03-moving-memory): Your compiler can check and run device loops, but render-cuda does not know them yet. A kernel on device 1 can only read device 1's memory, so the host has to move data there and bring results back...
- [A GEMM on two GPUs](https://sharpterminal.com/site/week10/04-sharded-gemm): You have written matrix multiply since week 3. Now you will split one across two devices, count every byte it moves, and add up a result that needs every device. Your compiler's render-cuda has to...
- [Training on several GPUs](https://sharpterminal.com/site/week10/05-training-on-many): In week 6 your compiler trained a model one batch at a time, on one device. Here the same training step runs on two GPUs: each works out the gradient for half the batch, and device 0 adds the halves...
- [Lab: multiple GPUs](https://sharpterminal.com/site/week10/06-lab): In this lab your compiler learns to run one program on several GPUs. It reads a device loop, proves that each device stays inside its shard, and prints CUDA that copies each device its memory, runs...

## Resources

- [Compiler bug hunt](https://sharpterminal.com/site/resources/bug-hunts): Ten real compiler bugs from weeks 1 to 9, each taken straight from the course's planted-bug suite. Read the failing test, then click the exact line in the compiler that breaks it.
- [Debugging your compiler](https://sharpterminal.com/site/resources/debugging): A red test is information. This page is the routine: read what the grader says, find out what the test is for, shrink it until the bug has nowhere to hide and compare with the oracle.
- [Glossary](https://sharpterminal.com/site/resources/glossary): Every term the course uses, in plain words, with the lessons that teach it. Search below, or jump to a letter.
- [When you're stuck, or curious](https://sharpterminal.com/site/resources/): The lessons teach each idea once. These pages are for the second pass: reviewing before a lab, finding out why a test fails, looking up a word or going further than the course does.
- [Python and OCaml, deeper](https://sharpterminal.com/site/resources/languages): The lessons teach enough of your language to build each week's compiler. This page is the next layer: the idioms and design patterns that make that compiler easier to write, the traps each language...
- [Quiz review](https://sharpterminal.com/site/resources/review): Questions you've answered come back here on a schedule, so they stick. You can also go through every quiz from a week, or only the ones you missed.

- [Week 10 study guide](https://sharpterminal.com/site/resources/week10): Week 10 runs one program on several GPUs. A device loop says which GPU runs which iterations, a rule decides whether each buffer is cut into shards or copied whole, and render-cuda writes the copies...
- [Week 2 study guide](https://sharpterminal.com/site/resources/week2): Week 2 adds floats and memory, and turns your compiler into one that prints C. The ideas are few but strict: f32 rounds after every op, memory comes in versions, every access has to be provably in...
- [Week 3 study guide](https://sharpterminal.com/site/resources/week3): Week 3 adds loops. A range is a loop counter, an end repeats an effect for every value of it, and your compiler learns to place each value at the right loop depth and print for loops. This page...
- [Week 4 study guide](https://sharpterminal.com/site/resources/week4): Week 4 lets you write whole-vector programs: elementwise ops on rank-1 values, reduce, expand and stage. Your compiler turns them back into week 3 loops by itself, a pass called rangeify. This page...
- [Week 5 study guide](https://sharpterminal.com/site/resources/week5): Week 5 lifts the rank limit. Values can have any rank while memory stays flat, and four movement ops (reshape, permute, pad, shrink) rearrange them without computing anything. A matmul or a...
- [Week 6 study guide](https://sharpterminal.com/site/resources/week6): Week 6 makes your compiler able to train. Four math functions are built from adds and multiplies, nine sugar ops expand into core ops, gradient walks the chain rule backward, and buffers can come...
- [Week 7 study guide](https://sharpterminal.com/site/resources/week7): Week 7 is about speed on a CPU. A range can say how its loop runs: as a plain loop, unrolled into registers or spread across threads. None of it changes a bit of any result, and from this week some...
- [Week 8 study guide](https://sharpterminal.com/site/resources/week8): Week 8 writes kernels the way a GPU runs them: a grid of blocks, each a group of threads with its own shared memory and a barrier. Two loop axes describe that, a stronger rule keeps threads and...
- [Week 9 study guide](https://sharpterminal.com/site/resources/week9): Week 9 makes GPU kernels fast without changing a bit: each thread keeps its own working set in registers, and warps hand 16×16 tile products to the tensor cores. With those two, the week builds a...
